title: Windows Security 4624 Successful Logon
content: Represents a successful logon. Inspect Subject and Target accounts, Logon Type, Authentication Package, source workstation and address, process or caller when present, and time. Benign examples include expected interactive, service, scheduled-task, or domain activity from managed hosts. Suspicion rises with a new source, unusual logon type, disabled or privileged account, impossible travel, or a success after clustered failures, but one 4624 is not proof. Correlate with 4625, 4648, 4672, 4768/4769, process creation, VPN/IdP and endpoint telemetry; compare the user and host baseline. Collect the complete event, identity context, source asset, time zone, related failures, and corroborating activity. Map only when behavior supports Valid Accounts or a remote-service technique.

title: Windows Security 4625 Failed Logon
content: Represents a failed logon attempt. Inspect target account, source workstation/address, Logon Type, authentication package, failure Status/SubStatus, caller process when available, and event volume. Benign causes include mistyped passwords, stale service credentials, mapped drives, scanners, and account changes. A single failure is weak evidence. One account targeted repeatedly suggests possible brute force; many accounts from one source suggests password spraying; many usernames with breached-password patterns may suggest credential stuffing. Require counts, distinct accounts, time window, source ownership, and successful follow-on activity before subtype or malicious classification. Correlate with 4624, 4740, 4776, VPN/IdP and endpoint data; preserve raw events and query coverage.

title: Windows Security 4648 Explicit Credentials
content: Records use of explicit credentials, commonly through RunAs, administration tools, or applications. Inspect the account whose credentials were used, the subject account, target server, process and caller, source host, and timing. Benign explanations include approved helpdesk work, deployment tooling, and a documented administrative workflow. Suspicion increases when an unusual user supplies privileged credentials to a new host, especially with 4688, 4624, remote service, or lateral movement evidence. Do not infer credential theft from this event alone. Collect the full event, process ancestry, ticket or change reference, target asset, and related authentication events.

title: Windows Security 4672 Special Privileges Assigned
content: Shows special privileges assigned to a new logon session. Inspect account, logon ID, privileges, source host, logon type, and nearby 4624 and 4688 events. Benign examples include domain administrators, Local System, backup agents, and security tooling. Treat it as context rather than an alert by itself; unusual account, source, time, or process behavior needs corroboration. Join on Logon ID where available, review privilege use and process ancestry, and preserve the complete session timeline.

title: Windows Security 4688 Process Creation
content: Represents a new process when process auditing is enabled. Inspect New Process Name, command line if enabled, Creator Process, token elevation, subject/logon ID, integrity level, signer, hash, user, host, and time. Benign patterns include installers, EDR, SCCM, Intune, software update agents, and administrator tools. Suspicious patterns include Office or browser spawning a script interpreter, encoded commands, temporary-path execution, unsigned binaries, or a rare parent-child chain. Correlate with Sysmon 1, 3, 11, 13, 22, downloads, persistence, and user activity. Missing command line or parent data is an evidence gap.

title: Windows Security 4697 Service Installed
content: Records a new service installation. Inspect service name, file path, service account, installer subject, start type, host, and timing. Benign examples include approved software deployment, drivers, EDR, backup, and patching. Suspicious indicators include a new service from a user-writable or temporary directory, unusual service account, remote administrative origin, unsigned binary, or a service created near credential or lateral-movement activity. Correlate 7045, 4688, Sysmon 1/11, file signature and hash, admin change records, and remote logons. Collect the event and service configuration; recommend containment only through authorized workflow.

title: Windows Security 4720 User Account Created
content: Represents creation of a local or domain user. Inspect creator, target account, domain, group memberships, account flags, workstation, and time. Benign explanations include onboarding, application identities, break-glass procedures, and automation with a documented ticket. Suspicion increases for a newly created enabled account, privileged membership, weak naming, unusual creator, or immediate logon/persistence. Correlate 4728/4732, 4624, 4672, directory changes, and endpoint activity. Require identity-owner confirmation and complete event evidence before classifying as malicious.

title: Windows Security 4728 Global Group Membership Change
content: Records a member added to a security-enabled global group. Inspect actor, member, group, domain, target domain controller, time, and change authorization. Benign examples include joiner-mover-leaver automation, approved role changes, and break-glass operations. Suspicion rises for privileged groups, unusual actor, off-hours change, newly created account, or subsequent privileged logon. Correlate 4720, 4624, 4672, 4732 and directory audit data. Confirm effective privileges and ticket evidence; membership change is high impact but not by itself proof of compromise.

title: Windows Security 4732 Local Group Membership Change
content: Records a member added to a local security-enabled group. Inspect member SID/name, group, actor, host, source logon, and time. Benign cases include endpoint management, software installation, and approved administrator access. Suspicion rises for a new account or unknown SID added to Administrators, especially with remote logon, service creation, or suspicious process activity. Correlate 4720, 4624, 4672, 4688 and endpoint group inventory. Validate the expected owner and change record before declaring compromise.

title: Windows Security 4740 Account Lockout
content: Represents an account lockout and often includes the caller computer. Inspect target account, caller host, preceding 4625/4776 failures, source IP, service accounts, scheduled tasks, mapped drives, and password age. Benign explanations include stale credentials in services, phones, VPN clients, or scripts. Repeated lockouts across many users or correlated successful logons may indicate attack activity. Distinguish one noisy client from distributed spraying using account and source distributions. Preserve the lockout event, failure window, caller identity, and baseline.

title: Windows Security 4768 Kerberos TGT Request
content: Represents a Kerberos TGT request. Inspect account, client address, service name, ticket encryption type, pre-authentication type, result code, and time. Benign variation can come from applications, domain controllers, legacy clients, and service accounts. Suspicion requires context such as unusual source, encryption downgrade, bursts of failures, privileged identity, or correlation with 4769 and endpoint activity. Do not call Kerberoasting from TGT activity alone; collect 4769 service-ticket requests and account/service context.

title: Windows Security 4769 Kerberos Service Ticket Request
topic: Kerberos service ticket and Kerberoasting analysis
content: Represents a Kerberos service-ticket request. Inspect requesting account, client address, service/SPN, encryption type, volume, distinct services, and time. Benign causes include normal application access, monitoring, backup, and service discovery. A burst of requests by one user or host across many SPNs, especially RC4 requests from a rare workstation, is a hypothesis for Kerberoasting—not proof. Correlate 4624, 4688, 4768, directory SPN ownership, PowerShell, and endpoint telemetry. Collect counts, baseline, account privilege, SPN owner, and raw event fields before mapping T1558.003.

title: Windows Security 4771 Kerberos Pre-Authentication Failed
content: Represents failed Kerberos pre-authentication. Inspect account, client address, failure code, encryption, domain controller, and time distribution. Benign explanations include stale credentials, clock skew, service restarts, and user mistakes. Many accounts from one source supports a spraying hypothesis; one account with high volume supports brute force; neither is conclusive without source ownership and success correlation. Correlate 4625, 4768, 4740, 4776, VPN/IdP, and service inventory. Preserve the time window and query coverage.

title: Windows Security 4776 NTLM Authentication
content: Represents NTLM credential validation, usually showing the authenticating account, workstation, and status. Inspect source workstation, account, result, protocol context, frequency, and whether the asset or application requires legacy NTLM. Benign explanations include legacy applications, file shares, scanners, and misconfigured services. Suspicion increases with unusual source, privileged account, repeated failures followed by success, or NTLM activity during lateral movement. Correlate 4624/4625, 4771, SMB/RDP/WMI telemetry, and baseline. Avoid equating NTLM use with credential theft; document verified evidence and protocol limitations.

title: System 7045 New Service Installed
source: Microsoft Windows Service Control Manager guidance
content: Records service installation in the System log. Inspect service name, image path, start type, service type, account, host, installer process, and time. Benign examples include patching, drivers, EDR, backup, and enterprise deployment. Suspicious patterns include a service from a temporary/user-writable path, encoded or unusual arguments, remote administration source, or close timing to 4688 and 4624 remote logons. Correlate Security 4697, process/file telemetry, signature and hash, and change records. Treat it as a high-value lead; scope before containment.

title: Windows Security 1102 Audit Log Cleared
content: Indicates the Security audit log was cleared. Inspect actor, host, time, preceding privileged logons, command/process telemetry, policy changes, collector continuity, and whether a documented maintenance action exists. Legitimate causes include authorized troubleshooting or rebuilds, but positive change evidence is required for a benign conclusion. Correlate 4688, 4672, 4624, service and policy events, endpoint tamper signals, and gaps in the central pipeline. Treat missing history as an evidence gap, preserve surviving telemetry, and escalate according to the authorized response plan.

title: Sysmon Event 1 Process Creation
content: Captures process GUID, image, command line, parent image/GUID, user, integrity, hashes, and file metadata when configured. Investigate the full ancestry, signer, prevalence, launch source, user intent, network children, and persistence. Benign explanations include installers, management agents, security tools, and update services. Suspicious parent-child chains, encoded commands, user-writable execution, or rare binaries require corroboration. Correlate Sysmon 3/11/13/22, Windows 4688, downloads, and authentication. Configuration gaps and missing fields must be reported.

title: Sysmon Event 3 Network Connection
content: Captures a network connection with process context when enabled. Inspect process image/GUID, user, source and destination IP/port, protocol, host role, DNS name, bytes and timing from companion telemetry. One connection or a reputation hit is not C2 proof. Correlate Sysmon 1, 22, proxy/TLS/firewall logs, periodicity, destination ownership, and baseline. Identify the owning process first; note NAT, shared infrastructure, missing DNS, and sensor coverage. Preserve the exact time window and flow direction.

title: Sysmon Event 7 Image Loaded
content: Records an image or DLL load when configured. Inspect loading process, loaded path, signer, signature status, hash, prevalence, architecture, and whether the path is expected for that application. Benign explanations include vendor plugins, browser extensions, and software updates. Suspicion rises for unsigned or mismatched DLLs in user-writable directories, search-order anomalies, or a rare process chain. Correlate Sysmon 1/11, module inventory, file reputation, and process behavior. A missing or unsigned image alone is not malware proof.

title: Sysmon Event 8 CreateRemoteThread
content: Records a remote thread created in another process. Inspect source and target images/GUIDs, user and integrity levels, start address/module/function, signer, hashes, and sequence of access/file events. Benign explanations include debuggers, accessibility tools, EDR, overlays, and legitimate instrumentation. Suspicion rises when an unusual unsigned source injects into a protected or unrelated target, especially with download, encoded execution, or C2 evidence. Correlate Sysmon 1/7/10/11 and EDR memory events. Require corroboration; this event is an indicator, not a verdict.

title: Sysmon Event 10 Process Access
topic: process access and credential theft indicators
content: Captures one process opening another process. Inspect source/target image and user, target process, GrantedAccess, call trace, signer, prevalence, and timing. Security products, debuggers, and legitimate administration may access processes, so LSASS access is a high-value lead rather than automatic credential dumping. Correlate Sysmon 1/8, file creation, suspicious handles, command lines, security product identity, and subsequent authentication or lateral movement. Preserve raw fields and identify whether the sensor logged the full sequence.

title: Sysmon Event 11 File Create
content: Records file creation with creating process, target path, user, and hashes when configured. Inspect path, extension, signer/hash, parent process, download source, subsequent execution, persistence, and prevalence. Benign explanations include installers, browser caches, SCCM/Intune, backup, and updates. Suspicion rises for a download followed quickly by execution, executable content in user-writable/temp paths, masqueraded names, or rare unsigned files. Correlate Sysmon 1/3/22, proxy, email, and persistence events; a suspicious file alone does not establish scope.

title: Sysmon Event 12 Registry Key Create or Delete
content: Records registry key creation or deletion. Inspect key path, event type, process, user, signer, value changes in nearby Event 13, and whether the key is a documented application setting. Benign examples include installers, profile management, and application cleanup. Suspicion increases for Run/RunOnce, unusual autorun locations, temporary paths, or a process with a suspicious parent. Correlate Sysmon 1/11/13 and startup inventory. Confirm persistence behavior and owner before classification.

title: Sysmon Event 13 Registry Value Set
content: Records a registry value modification. Inspect full key/value, data, writing process, user, signer, hash, and first-seen history. Benign explanations include software installation, updates, endpoint management, and browser/application settings. Suspicion rises for autorun keys pointing to user-writable, temporary, script, or unsigned content, particularly when followed by execution. Correlate Sysmon 1/11/12, Windows process events, and startup inventory. Preserve exact data and distinguish a persistence-capable value from confirmed execution.

title: Sysmon Event 22 DNS Query
content: Records a DNS query with process context when enabled. Inspect queried name, response/status, process image/GUID, user, resolver, frequency, NXDOMAIN rate, first-seen history, and domain context. Benign causes include browsers, CDNs, telemetry, software updates, and security tools. Suspicion rises with high-entropy or newly observed domains, periodic queries, rare process ownership, or DNS followed by network and execution activity. Correlate proxy/firewall, Sysmon 1/3, endpoint, and baseline. Domain reputation alone is insufficient for C2 classification.

title: Authentication Failure Subtype Analysis
topic: brute force password spraying credential stuffing and mistakes
content: Classify only from distributions and context. Single-account brute force has many attempts against one account; password spraying has one or a few passwords across many accounts and often many sources or a low rate per account; credential stuffing uses many account identifiers and commonly external application telemetry; user error is low-volume and consistent with the user's normal device; service failures repeat from a known application or host. Calculate attempts, distinct accounts, distinct sources, success-after-failure, lockouts, and time window. Correlate 4624/4625, 4740, 4771/4776, VPN/IdP, device and geo. Keep subtype UNKNOWN when evidence is insufficient.

title: Authentication Risk Context
topic: impossible travel new device geography and privileged activity
log_source: Identity provider and endpoint authentication logs
content: Treat impossible travel, unusual geography, new source IP, new device, and privileged activity as risk signals. Validate time zones, VPN egress, mobile networks, proxies, shared NAT, travel, device enrollment, MFA result, session continuity, and user confirmation. A new location or device is not proof of account compromise; positive benign evidence is required for BENIGN. Correlate successful logon with preceding failures, token/session events, endpoint process activity, mailbox or cloud actions, and peer baseline. Record exact sources and missing identity telemetry; use UNKNOWN when travel calculation or device attribution is unreliable.

title: DNS Investigation Workflow
content: For a domain, preserve the queried name, resolver, process and user when available, response, time, frequency, first-seen history, registration context, hosting, and baseline. Reputation and newly observed status are enrichment, not verdicts; CDNs, SaaS, and newly deployed business services can be benign. Correlate DNS with Sysmon 1/3, proxy/TLS, firewall, downloads, and periodicity. Identify the owning process and asset. Collect raw queries and coverage; a zero-result query may reflect retention, resolver choice, or missing sensor rather than absence.

title: HTTP HTTPS and TLS Investigation
topic: web protocols proxy logs and certificates
log_source: Proxy, firewall, TLS and endpoint telemetry
content: Inspect owning process, user, URL/host, destination IP, SNI, certificate subject and issuer, validity, protocol, user agent, request timing, response codes, and bytes. Benign alternatives include browsers, APIs, CDNs, update agents, and certificate rotation. Suspicion requires correlated process, domain, periodicity, unusual destination, or payload behavior; one HTTPS connection, certificate oddity, or reputation hit is insufficient. Correlate DNS, Sysmon 1/3/22, proxy, firewall, endpoint and baseline. Note TLS inspection and proxy blind spots explicitly.

title: Beaconing and Large Outbound Transfer Analysis
log_source: NetFlow, proxy, firewall and endpoint telemetry
content: Test beaconing with repeated connections, interval and jitter, destination stability, process ownership, user/host role, bytes and direction, and historical baseline. Test possible exfiltration with volume relative to host and peer baseline, data source, archive/staging events, destination ownership, protocol, and time correlation. Backups, replication, cloud sync, video, updates, and proxies are benign alternatives. A periodic connection or large transfer alone is not C2 or exfiltration proof. Correlate process/file/archive activity, DNS, proxy and identity context; document missing payload visibility.

title: Linux auth.log SSH Investigation
topic: SSH failures successes and brute force
source: Linux audit and OpenSSH defensive methodology
content: Review SSH failed and accepted authentication entries with timestamp, account, source IP, authentication method, destination, PAM result, and session/command context. Compare one-account volume versus many-account distribution, known scanners, allowlisted administration, and host baseline. A successful login after failures needs correlation with user/device ownership, key inventory, sudo, process, and outbound activity. Preserve log timezone, rotation state, and query window. Conceptual read-only checks include reviewing auth.log/journal, active sessions, process inventory, SSH configuration, and authorized_keys; do not run destructive remediation commands automatically.

title: Linux Persistence Investigation
log_source: auditd, auth logs, systemd and filesystem telemetry
content: Inspect user and system cron entries, systemd units/timers, service executable paths, enablement, owner, creation time, SSH authorized_keys, and recent file/process activity. Benign alternatives include package managers, monitoring, backups, configuration management, and deployment. Suspicion rises for hidden names, user-writable paths, encoded shell commands, newly added keys, or persistence immediately after suspicious access. Correlate auth.log, auditd, process tree, outbound connections, package history, and change records. Collect file metadata and content through authorized read-only procedures; recommend removal only through approved response.

title: Linux sudo Privilege and Process Investigation
topic: sudo abuse privilege escalation and suspicious processes
log_source: auditd, auth.log, sudo logs and process telemetry
content: Correlate sudo authorization, invoking user, target user, command, TTY, source session, parent process, executable path, file owner and network activity. Check setuid binaries, capabilities, shell history with caution, and new accounts/services. Benign explanations include automation, administrators, package operations, and monitoring; history can be absent or tampered with and is not complete evidence. Suspicion requires unusual account/command/path plus corroboration. Use read-only process and log inspection, preserve permissions and timestamps, and report gaps caused by audit configuration or rotation.

title: Suspicious File and Hash Analysis
topic: SHA256 reputation static and dynamic indicators
content: Calculate or verify SHA256 from observed evidence and record path, host, user, signer, prevalence, parent-child process, command line, network, persistence, and execution time. Reputation hits are useful leads but may reflect shared files, false positives, outdated verdicts, or one sample; a hash alone does not define incident scope. Static indicators include imports, strings, signature and metadata; dynamic indicators include child processes, injection, DNS, network, file and registry changes. Correlate across hosts and users, preserve sample provenance, and use UNKNOWN when execution or ownership is unverified.

title: Malware Behavior Correlation
topic: obfuscation LOLBins temporary execution and injection
content: Treat obfuscation, encoded commands, LOLBins, unsigned binaries, temporary-directory execution, download-then-run, and injection as behavior indicators. Inspect decoded intent only in an approved analysis environment, signer and path, parent/child chain, file origin, user, network, persistence, and host prevalence. Benign alternatives include installers, support tools, security products, and testing. Require multiple correlated indicators before calling malware; one LOLBin or unsigned file is not enough. Preserve command lines and hashes, map only the behavior supported by telemetry, and separate observed facts from interpretation.

title: False Positives from Enterprise and Security Tools
topic: PowerShell scheduled tasks SCCM Intune installers backups and updates
content: For suspicious PowerShell, scheduled tasks, temporary paths, installers, SCCM, Intune, backup agents, security products, remote administration, signed vendor binaries, and test/sandbox hosts, document both hypotheses. Validate publisher/signature, exact path, parent process, command purpose, approved host/user scope, maintenance window, deployment job, prevalence, and network behavior. A legitimate label requires positive ownership or change evidence; suspicious appearance alone remains UNKNOWN. If tuning is needed, use narrow entity-aware conditions and test against recent benign and known-bad samples.

title: Evidence-Based Detection Engineering and Tuning
topic: rule validation thresholds exceptions and ATT&CK coverage
content: Analyze rule intent, data prerequisites, field mappings, time window, threshold, entity distribution, and ATT&CK mapping before tuning. Build a labeled sample of true positives, benign cases, and unknowns; compare baseline and host/user distribution; simulate the proposed logic; then monitor precision, recall proxies, missed detections, and alert volume. Prefer exact approved process/path, host, user, signer, or narrow time/entity conditions over broad exclusions. Validate in staging or a controlled period, preserve rollback, and document residual risk. Do not invent fields: verify actual integration mappings.

title: Incident Playbook Phishing
log_source: Email, identity, endpoint and proxy telemetry
content: Alert summary: preserve sender, recipients, subject, timestamps, URLs, attachment hashes, delivery and click status. Initial facts must distinguish delivered, opened, clicked, executed, and authenticated. Collect message headers, related recipients, endpoint process tree, file and DNS/proxy activity, and identity events. Test benign campaign, security simulation, and malicious delivery hypotheses. Severity rises with execution, credential submission, privileged target, or spread. Escalate when multiple users or endpoint evidence exists. Evidence gaps include missing mail telemetry or URL detonation. Containment, reset, and remediation remain recommendations for authorized responders.

title: Incident Playbook Suspicious PowerShell
content: Alert summary: capture host, user, exact command line, script block or AMSI data when authorized, parent/child tree, signer, path, hash, network, and persistence. Initial facts are separate from observations. Consider administration, SCCM/Intune, security tooling, testing, and malicious download/execution hypotheses. Correlate 4688/Sysmon 1, 3, 11, 13, 22, identity, and proxy. Escalate for encoded or obfuscated intent plus external download, credential access, injection, persistence, or multi-host spread. Missing script content or endpoint coverage must be explicit; response actions require authorization.

title: Incident Playbooks Brute Force Password Spraying and Account Compromise
content: Alert summary: define account/source/time scope and preserve raw failures, successes, lockouts, MFA and device data. Determine subtype from distributions, not alert names: one account, many accounts, external credential reuse, user error, or service failure. Correlate successful logons after failures, privileged activity, device posture, geo/VPN, process and mailbox/cloud actions. Benign hypotheses require user, service owner, or approved scanner evidence; malicious hypotheses require corroboration. Escalate for confirmed unauthorized success, privileged access, spread, or multiple affected identities. Password reset, disablement, blocking, and containment are recommendations until an authorized workflow acts.

title: Incident Playbooks Suspicious Network C2 and Exfiltration
topic: network connection possible C2 and data transfer
content: Alert summary: identify owning process, user, host, destination, DNS context, protocol, TLS, timing, bytes, and baseline. Collect flow/proxy/DNS records, process tree, file/hash, persistence, and peer/host spread. Consider CDN, update, backup, cloud sync, monitoring, and business API hypotheses alongside C2 or exfiltration. One connection, reputation hit, periodicity signal, or large transfer alone is insufficient. Escalate when process, destination, repeated timing, payload/staging, and identity evidence converge. Note encrypted/payload visibility gaps. Network blocking or host isolation remains an authorized-response recommendation.

title: Elastic Splunk and Sentinel Investigation Portability
topic: platform-aware fields timelines entities and baselines
content: Start from the platform's verified schema and actual returned fields. Elastic Security may use ECS and ES|QL/KQL depending on workflow; Splunk commonly uses CIM/SPL; Sentinel commonly uses ASIM/KQL, but integrations vary. Do not invent field names: inspect mappings, event examples, source type/table, and normalized versus vendor fields. Pivot by verified host, user, process, IP, domain, hash, and time; preserve query window, index/sourcetype/table, and empty-result limitations. Use alert/notable context as a lead, timeline correlation and entity baselines as evidence, and map ATT&CK only after behavior is supported.

title: SIEM Alert Triage and Evidence Handoff
topic: alert facts timeline evidence gaps and escalation
content: For every alert record alert ID/rule/time, raw facts, derived observations, benign and malicious hypotheses, evidence supporting each, missing evidence, scope, confidence, and next action. Severity and MITRE labels prioritize work but are not proof. Correlate host, user, process, network, authentication, persistence, and baseline data across a bounded window. A zero-result search means coverage or mapping may be insufficient. BENIGN requires positive legitimacy evidence; MALICIOUS requires corroboration; otherwise use UNKNOWN. Handoff should include exact sources, queries or pivots used, timestamps, and authorized escalation criteria.

title: MITRE Initial Access: Phishing Remote Services and Valid Accounts
topic: phishing malicious attachments links external remote services valid accounts
log_source: Email, identity, VPN and endpoint telemetry
content: Investigate delivery, user interaction, external remote-service login, and valid-account use as separate behaviors. Useful telemetry includes message headers and attachment/link events, IdP/VPN authentication, device posture, endpoint execution, and proxy/DNS. Benign alternatives include security simulations, approved remote access, travel, VPN egress, and shared services. Require delivery or login evidence plus identity/device/process correlation before classification. Map the specific sub-technique supported; a rule label or reputation result is not proof.

title: MITRE Execution: Command Shell Scripting User Execution and Scheduled Tasks
topic: command shell scripting user execution scheduled task execution
content: Inspect process command line, parent, user, script content where authorized, task name/action/author, trigger, path, signer, and host baseline. Benign alternatives include management agents, installers, login scripts, and scheduled maintenance. Suspicion requires unusual ancestry, encoded/obfuscated intent, user-writable paths, external download, or persistence correlation. Collect process/task events and map only the specific supported sub-technique. User execution requires evidence the user opened or ran content, not just delivery.

title: MITRE Persistence: Run Keys Scheduled Tasks Services Cron and SSH Keys
log_source: Endpoint, registry, service, cron and SSH telemetry
content: Review autorun keys/startup, scheduled tasks, services, cron/systemd, and SSH authorized_keys with creator, path, owner, signer, timestamps, trigger, and execution evidence. Benign alternatives are deployment, patching, monitoring, backups, and approved administration. Suspicion increases for hidden names, user-writable payloads, new keys/accounts, or persistence after suspicious access. Correlate process, file, registry, authentication, and outbound events. A persistence configuration is not proof it executed; preserve evidence and recommend response only through authorization.

title: MITRE Privilege Escalation: Exploitation Elevation and Services
topic: exploitation abuse elevation control and service-based escalation
log_source: Endpoint, Windows Security and Linux audit telemetry
content: Establish the initial user, transition to elevated context, vulnerable or misconfigured component, and resulting privileged process. Inspect token/integrity, exploit or UAC evidence, sudo/audit records, service path/permissions, parent chain, file/hash and host baseline. Benign administration and installers are alternatives. Do not infer exploitation from privilege assignment alone; require corroboration and preserve pre/post activity. Map the exact mechanism and document missing exploit telemetry.

title: MITRE Defense Evasion: Obfuscation Masquerading LOLBins and Impair Defenses
topic: obfuscation indicator removal signed binary proxy and defense impairment
log_source: Endpoint, process, audit and security-product telemetry
content: Inspect exact command/data, signer, path, parent, user, file origin, security-control status, and event gaps. Encoded content, renamed binaries, LOLBins, log clearing, and impaired controls have legitimate administrative and testing explanations. Require intent plus correlated execution, network, credential, persistence, or scope evidence. Map the supported behavior separately; do not treat a signed binary or ATT&CK label as malicious by itself. Preserve surviving telemetry and identify collection gaps.

title: MITRE Credential Access: Dumping Kerberoasting Brute Force and NTLM
topic: credential dumping Kerberos abuse password attacks and NTLM
log_source: Identity, Windows Security and endpoint telemetry
content: Use the event-specific workflows for LSASS/process access, 4769 SPN requests, failed authentication distributions, and NTLM context. Require source process/account, volume, baseline, target, and follow-on authentication or lateral movement evidence. Security tools and legacy applications are benign alternatives. A credential-access alert, hash, or one ticket request is not sufficient to claim theft or incident scope. Preserve raw events, map the narrowest supported technique, and record evidence gaps.

title: MITRE Discovery and Lateral Movement Investigation
topic: accounts processes systems files network services remote services RDP SMB WMI
log_source: Endpoint, Windows, network and authentication telemetry
content: Investigate discovery commands and remote access as a sequence: initiating user/process, targets, protocol, source/destination, authentication, execution, and resulting activity. Benign alternatives include inventory, vulnerability scanning, helpdesk, deployment, and administration. Require unusual scope, source, account, timing, or correlated execution for suspicious classification. Correlate 4624/4648/4672, 4688, Sysmon 3, service creation, SMB/RDP/WMI and baseline. One scan or remote login is not lateral movement proof.

title: MITRE Command and Control and Exfiltration Investigation
topic: web DNS encrypted channels beaconing web service and outbound transfer
log_source: Network, proxy, DNS, TLS and endpoint telemetry
content: Correlate owning process, user, destination, DNS, TLS/SNI, URL, timing, bytes, upload direction, staging files, and baseline. Benign alternatives include browsers, SaaS, cloud sync, updates, backups, and APIs. Reputation, encryption, periodicity, or large transfer alone is insufficient. Require multiple independent signals and preserve payload visibility limitations. Map web/DNS/encrypted channel or exfiltration only where the observed protocol and direction support it; response actions need authorization.
